\subsection{Capability-Safety Anti-correlation}\label{sec:tsr_car}

The displacement analysis in Section~\ref{sec:fake_safety} reveals a striking pattern at the aggregate level: models with higher task capability systematically report lower collision avoidance rates. Pi0.5 achieves a TSR of 74.7\,$\pm$\,1.5\% but a CAR of only 26.8\,$\pm$\,1.6\%, while Pi0-based methods (LoRA baseline, Full-FT, and A1-LoRA) report TSR $\leq$ 0.5\% alongside CAR values of 82--91.5\%. The anti-correlation is consistent across all three Pi0.5 seeds (TSR 73--76\%, CAR 25--28\%) and across Pi0 variants regardless of whether an SDF loss is applied. We observe that models capable of executing tasks also move the robot into configurations where collisions become possible, while models that fail to act avoid collisions by default.

Figure~\ref{fig:tsr_car_scatter} plots all evaluated configurations in TSR-CAR space. Two clusters emerge. Pi0-family methods occupy the upper-left region: high CAR, near-zero TSR. As established in Section~\ref{sec:fake_safety}, over 99\% of their safe episodes are fake safe, placing this cluster in what we term the \emph{fake safety zone}. Pi0.5, by contrast, sits in the lower-right region: high TSR, low CAR. Its collisions reflect genuine robot motion through the workspace. The two clusters are separated by a gap that no existing method occupies, a region that would require both meaningful task execution and reliable obstacle avoidance.

This spatial structure has a direct implication for metric interpretation. A model that reports high CAR but near-zero TSR provides no evidence of collision avoidance capability; its safety score is an artifact of inaction. CAR is informative only when conditioned on sufficient task capability. We note that the TSR-CAR plane offers a more complete picture than either metric alone: the upper-right quadrant (high TSR, high CAR) represents genuinely safe and capable behavior, while the upper-left quadrant is accessible through action collapse without any safety mechanism.

Early results from a Pi0.5 model augmented with A1-level SDF training (10K-step checkpoint) suggest that this gap is not inherent. This configuration achieves TSR of 47--49\% with CAR of 56--58\% and a frozen-action rate of 0\%, placing it in the previously unoccupied central region of Figure~\ref{fig:tsr_car_scatter}. We defer detailed analysis of this model to Section~\ref{sec:a1_pi05}, but note here that its position confirms the trade-off is a property of current models, not a fundamental constraint. Genuine collision avoidance requires a model that both moves and avoids, a combination that raw CAR cannot distinguish from one that simply does not move.

\subsection{End-Effector-Only SDF Cannot Ensure Full-Body Safety}\label{sec:ee_only}

The analyses in Sections~\ref{sec:fake_safety} and~\ref{sec:tsr_car} identify action collapse and fake safety as pervasive problems, but leave open a natural question: could a sufficiently accurate SDF prediction still enable effective runtime refinement? To isolate the SDF representation itself from prediction quality, we construct an oracle experiment. We replace the learned SDF network with the ground-truth signed distance field computed directly from the known obstacle geometry. This oracle represents the theoretical upper bound of end-effector-only SDF refinement: it eliminates prediction error entirely, providing the refinement module with a perfect distance signal at every timestep. If the SDF refinement paradigm is sound, oracle performance should exceed that of unrefined baselines by a wide margin.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Oracle SDF refinement with ground-truth distance fields (160 episodes, 4 tasks $\times$ 40). All three variants achieve lower CAR than unrefined baselines (LoRA 82.0\%, Full-FT 83.0\%), and fake safe rates remain above 96\%.}
\label{tab:oracle}
\vspace{2pt}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
Method & TSR (\%) & CAR (\%) & Fake Safe (\%) & Refines/ep \\
\midrule
LoRA baseline (no refine) & 0.0 & 82.0 & 99.4 & -- \\
Full-FT baseline (no refine) & 0.5 & 83.0 & -- & -- \\
\midrule
Oracle-adaptive (GT, dyn.\ $\alpha$) & 0.0 & 75.0 & 98.3 & 14.2 \\
Oracle-fixed (GT, $\alpha{=}0.005$) & 0.0 & 73.1 & 98.3 & 14.8 \\
Oracle-feature (GT, feat.\ space) & 0.0 & 76.9 & 96.7 & 241.7 \\
\midrule
A3 learned SDF & 0.0 & 74.5 & -- & 0.0 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:oracle} reports the results. All three oracle variants achieve CAR below that of the unrefined baselines. The best oracle (Oracle-feature, 76.9\%) falls 5.1 percentage points below the LoRA baseline (82.0\%) and 6.1 points below Full-FT (83.0\%). The adaptive and fixed-step variants perform worse still, at 75.0\% and 73.1\% respectively. These results are not marginal: the refinement module with perfect distance information produces more collisions than doing nothing at all. The fake safe rate tells a complementary story. Oracle-adaptive and Oracle-fixed both register 98.3\% fake safe episodes (118 of 120 and 115 of 117 safe episodes, respectively), while Oracle-feature registers 96.7\% (119 of 123). Ground-truth SDF refinement does not reduce action collapse; the vast majority of safe episodes remain attributable to inaction rather than obstacle avoidance.

The per-task breakdown in Figure~\ref{fig:oracle_bar} reveals additional structure. On task~1, the most collision-prone task where the LoRA baseline achieves only 46.0\% CAR, Oracle-adaptive reaches 55.0\% and Oracle-feature reaches 47.5\%, a modest improvement consistent with a scenario where the end-effector is the primary collision body. On tasks~0, 2, and~3, all oracle variants produce lower CAR than the baseline: Oracle-adaptive drops from 96.0\% to 82.5\% on task~0 and from 98.0\% to 77.5\% on task~2. The refinement gradient, which pushes the end-effector away from the obstacle surface, perturbs the planned trajectory in ways that increase collisions elsewhere on the robot arm.

This failure mode is structural. The SDF refinement paradigm as formulated in prior work~\cite{hu2025vlsa} computes the signed distance from the end-effector to the nearest obstacle surface and applies a gradient step to increase this distance when it falls below a safety threshold. The gradient operates exclusively on the end-effector position; no distance constraint applies to the remaining links of the robot arm. When the gradient pushes the end-effector away from an obstacle, the resulting joint-space displacement can rotate intermediate links toward or through the obstacle volume. The refinement thus trades one collision for another, with no mechanism to detect or prevent the substitution. The feature-space oracle makes this coupling problem explicit. It applies the SDF gradient in the policy's latent action space rather than in Cartesian coordinates, and fires on nearly every timestep (241.7 refinements per episode versus 14.2 for action-space variants). Yet its gradient magnitudes are extremely small (0.004--0.006, compared to 0.18--0.49 in action space), and the resulting CAR (76.9\%) shows no significant advantage over the action-space oracles. The latent space lacks a direct geometric relationship to full-body configuration; small perturbations in feature space do not reliably translate into collision-free joint trajectories.

The A3 model with a learned SDF head illustrates the complementary failure. In this configuration, the SDF prediction network never outputs a distance below the refinement threshold across any of the 160 evaluation episodes, resulting in zero refinement steps. The learned SDF has calibrated its predictions to avoid triggering the safety mechanism, effectively reducing the model to an unrefined baseline (CAR of 74.5\%, consistent with the oracle range). The refinement module, even if it could improve safety, is never activated.

These results establish that end-effector-only SDF is a structural limitation, not merely an engineering gap. Perfect distance information does not compensate for the absence of full-body collision awareness. Any refinement scheme that monitors only the end-effector position will remain blind to arm-body collisions, which constitute the dominant failure mode in manipulation tasks where the robot must reach around or past obstacles. Effective collision avoidance for VLA models will require representations that account for the geometric extent of the entire manipulator, not only its tip.

\section{Experimental Framework}\label{sec:framework}

### §4.1 Benchmark and Evaluation Protocol
- **SafeLIBERO**~\cite{hu2025vlsa}: 基于 LIBERO~\cite{liu2023libero} 的碰撞安全评估扩展

### §4.2 Evaluation Metrics
**Standard metrics:**
- **Task Success Rate (TSR)**: fraction of episodes where manipulation task completed successfully
- **Collision Avoidance Rate (CAR)**: fraction of episodes with no collision with non-target objects

**Proposed metric (核心方法论贡献):**
- **Displacement-Filtered CAR (CAR_f)**: 排除 action-collapsed episodes
- 定义 action collapse: max EE displacement d_max(e) < τ_d = 0.1mm
- 公式（已在 §5.1 给出，这里给出 formal definition）:
  CAR_f = |{e : safe(e) ∧ d_max(e) ≥ τ_d}| / |{e : d_max(e) ≥ τ_d}|
- 动机简述（1-2 句）：标准 CAR 不区分 "safe because avoided" vs "safe because frozen"
- 注意：不要与 §5.1 重复太多推导。§4.2 给 formal definition + 动机；§5.1 给 empirical evidence

**Additional metrics（简要提及）:**
- **Frozen Rate**: fraction of episodes with d_max < τ_d（衡量 action collapse 程度）
- **SSR (Simultaneous Success Rate)**: TSR ∩ CAR（同时完成任务且无碰撞）

\section{Introduction}

Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models unify visual perception, language understanding, and continuous action generation in a single architecture. Models such as $\pi_0$~\cite{black2024pi0}, OpenVLA~\cite{kim2024openvla}, and RT-2~\cite{brohan2023rt2} can follow diverse natural language instructions across manipulation tasks. As these models move toward real-world deployment, a critical failure mode has emerged: frequent collisions with non-target objects in cluttered environments. The demonstration data used for training typically features unobstructed workspaces, and the resulting policies acquire no explicit incentive to maintain clearance from nearby surfaces. Collisions cause task failure, risk damage to the robot and its surroundings, and represent a central barrier to safe deployment. The SafeLIBERO benchmark~\cite{hu2025vlsa}, comprising 32 collision scenarios across 1,600 evaluation episodes, was introduced to systematically quantify this problem and confirms that even high-performing VLAs exhibit substantial collision rates when non-target objects surround the manipulation target.

Several recent methods target collision avoidance in VLAs. AEGIS~\cite{hu2025vlsa} applies post-hoc Control Barrier Function (CBF) corrections to already-generated trajectories and reports an average Collision Avoidance Rate (CAR) of 77.85\% across SafeLIBERO scenarios without additional training. SafeVLA~\cite{zhang2025safevla}%[CITE-CHECK] formulates safety as a constrained Markov Decision Process and reduces safety violations by 83.58\% through reward shaping during reinforcement learning. CoFreeVLA~\cite{cofreeevla2026}%[CITE-CHECK] trains a risk estimator for dual-arm settings that halts execution when predicted collision risk exceeds a threshold. In our own experiments, a Pi0 model fine-tuned with an auxiliary Signed Distance Field (SDF) loss (referred to as A1-LoRA) achieves 91.5\% CAR on SafeLIBERO. These methods share a common evaluation pattern: they report high CAR as evidence of effective collision avoidance. The numbers appear compelling, and the implicit assumption across this emerging literature is that high CAR reflects genuine obstacle avoidance behavior.

For the Pi0-family models we evaluate, this assumption does not hold. Their CAR values are systematically contaminated by \emph{action collapse}, a phenomenon in which the VLA ceases to produce meaningful motion. We argue that the underlying mechanism, action collapse inflating displacement-based safety metrics, is likely present in any VLA susceptible to mode collapse, though our direct evidence comes from the Pi0 family. When we examine the end-effector displacement of the 732 episodes that A1-LoRA classifies as ``safe,'' 99.6\% exhibit a maximum displacement below 0.1\,mm. The robot did not avoid obstacles; it avoided motion altogether. This contamination is not specific to A1-LoRA or to SDF-based approaches. The LoRA baseline (no collision avoidance objective) achieves 82\% CAR with 99.4\% of its safe episodes below the displacement threshold. Pi0.5, a more capable model from the same family, exhibits the same pattern: 98.2\% of its safe episodes are fake safe. We acknowledge that action collapse itself is a well-documented failure mode of undertrained or distribution-shifted models, and its existence alone would not warrant a dedicated analysis. What is non-trivial is the \emph{consequence}: action collapse silently inflates the primary safety metric used to evaluate collision avoidance methods. Downstream researchers who compare methods based on reported CAR values will draw incorrect conclusions about relative safety. Models that collapse more severely will paradoxically appear safer, and genuinely unsafe models may be deployed on the basis of contaminated evaluations. We propose the displacement-filtered CAR (CAR$_\text{f}$), which excludes episodes with sub-threshold displacement from both numerator and denominator, as a corrective metric that separates genuine avoidance from inaction.

The fake safety problem connects to two deeper structural issues. First, task capability and collision avoidance are anti-correlated under current evaluation practice. Pi0.5 achieves a TSR of 74.7\,$\pm$\,1.5\% but a CAR of only 26.8\,$\pm$\,1.6\%, while Pi0-based methods report CAR of 82--91.5\% alongside TSR $\leq$ 0.5\%. The explanation is mechanical: a model that moves the robot through the workspace encounters obstacles; a model that does not move encounters none. CAR is therefore informative only when conditioned on sufficient task capability, and the TSR-CAR plane reveals that no current method occupies the upper-right quadrant where both metrics are high. Second, end-effector-only SDF refinement, the most direct geometric approach to collision avoidance, has a structural defect. We construct oracle experiments that replace the learned SDF network with ground-truth signed distance fields computed from simulation geometry. All three oracle variants achieve \emph{lower} CAR than unrefined baselines (best oracle: 76.9\% vs.\ LoRA baseline: 82.0\%). The SDF gradient pushes the end-effector away from obstacles, but the resulting joint-space displacement rotates intermediate arm links toward or through obstacle volumes. Perfect distance information at the end-effector cannot compensate for the absence of full-body collision awareness. A preliminary result provides a constructive counterpoint: a Pi0.5 model augmented with training-time SDF supervision (10K-step checkpoint) achieves CAR of 56--58\% with TSR of 47--49\% and a frozen-action rate of 0\%, placing it in the previously empty central region of the TSR-CAR plane which suggests that genuine collision avoidance is achievable when the base model retains sufficient capability.

Our contributions are as follows:
\begin{itemize}
    \item We identify the fake safety problem in VLA collision avoidance evaluation: action collapse systematically inflates Collision Avoidance Rate, and we find that 98--99\% of safe episodes across multiple methods and model scales are attributable to inaction rather than obstacle avoidance. We propose displacement-filtered CAR (CAR$_\text{f}$) as a corrective metric (Section~\ref{sec:fake_safety}).
    \item We demonstrate that model capability and reported collision avoidance are anti-correlated under standard CAR evaluation. Models that execute tasks collide more because they move, while action-collapsed models receive inflated safety scores, rendering cross-method comparisons on raw CAR misleading (Section~\ref{sec:tsr_car}).
    \item Through ground-truth SDF oracle experiments, we establish that end-effector-only SDF refinement is a structural limitation: even perfect distance information cannot prevent full-body collisions, as gradients that repel the end-effector simultaneously drive arm links into obstacle volumes (Section~\ref{sec:ee_only}).

\end{itemize}

\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}

\subsection{Collision-Safe VLA Methods}\label{sec:rw_collision}

Recent methods for collision avoidance in VLAs fall into three categories. \textbf{Post-hoc correction} approaches modify policy outputs before execution. AEGIS~\cite{hu2025vlsa} applies Control Barrier Function corrections to VLA actions based on open-set detection and monocular depth estimation, and reports 77.85\% CAR on SafeLIBERO without additional training. iKinQP-RL~\cite{spalter2024ikinqp} enforces collision constraints through inverse-kinematics quadratic programming at runtime. CoFreeVLA~\cite{cofreeevla2026}%[CITE-CHECK]
trains a risk estimator that halts dual-arm execution when predicted collision probability exceeds a threshold.

\textbf{Constrained optimization} embeds safety into training. SafeVLA~\cite{zhang2025safevla}%[CITE-CHECK]
formulates collision avoidance as a Constrained MDP and reports an 83.58\% reduction in safety violations through reward shaping.

\textbf{Inference-time guidance} steers the generative process toward safe trajectories without retraining. Li et al.~\cite{li2024langguided} train an object-centric diffusion policy on 3D point clouds and inject collision costs during denoising. CAPE~\cite{yang2025cape} expands the trajectory distribution through context-aware priors and iterative refinement.

These methods differ in mechanism but share a common evaluation pattern: all report Collision Avoidance Rate as primary evidence of safety. None examine whether the measured CAR reflects genuine obstacle avoidance or conflates it with other behaviors. Our analysis (Section~\ref{sec:fake_safety}) reveals that this conflation is severe in the Pi0 family: 98--99\% of safe episodes are attributable to inaction rather than planned avoidance. We do not challenge the technical contributions of these methods; we identify a validity gap in the metric on which they rely, and propose a filtered variant (CAR$_\text{f}$) that separates genuine avoidance from frozen behavior.

\subsection{Signed Distance Fields in Robot Manipulation}\label{sec:rw_sdf}

Signed Distance Fields encode the distance from a query point to the nearest obstacle surface, where the sign indicates free space (positive) or penetration (negative). DeepSDF~\cite{park2019deepsdf} established neural SDF prediction as a compact shape representation. iSDF~\cite{ortiz2022isdf} extended this to incremental scene reconstruction for real-time robot perception. DiffCo~\cite{zhi2021diffco} introduced differentiable collision checking through learned distance fields and showed that gradient-based trajectory optimization can enforce collision constraints. VoxPoser~\cite{huang2023voxposer} composes 3D value maps from language model outputs for manipulation planning, with avoidance maps that encode obstacle information in volumetric form.

SDF-based collision detection is well validated in classical motion planning. The natural question is whether this effectiveness transfers to VLA action refinement, where the SDF gradient modifies predicted end-effector actions to increase obstacle clearance. Our oracle experiments (Section~\ref{sec:ee_only}) test this directly by replacing the learned SDF network with ground-truth distance fields computed from simulation geometry, which eliminates all prediction error. The results reveal a structural limitation of end-effector-only refinement: all three oracle variants produce more collisions than unrefined baselines, because the gradient that repels the end-effector simultaneously rotates arm links into obstacle volumes. The problem is not SDF accuracy but application scope. Full-body collision avoidance requires distance information along the entire kinematic chain, not only at the tool tip.

\subsection{Evaluation Reliability in Robot Learning}\label{sec:rw_eval}

Concerns about whether standard metrics measure what they claim to measure have a long history in ML evaluation. Benchmark saturation and annotation artifact exploitation in NLP demonstrated that high scores can reflect dataset properties rather than target capabilities~\cite{placeholder_metric_reliability}. Goodhart's law (a measure ceases to be informative once it becomes an optimization target) has been documented in reinforcement learning settings where agents exploit reward proxies rather than solve intended tasks~\cite{placeholder_goodhart_rl}. These cases share a common structure: a metric that appears to measure capability $X$ in fact measures a confound $Y$, and the discrepancy remains invisible until the aggregate score is decomposed.

The confound in VLA safety evaluation is action collapse, a phenomenon related to mode collapse in generative models. Diffusion-based robot policies can collapse to the mean of multi-modal action distributions~\cite{chi2023diffusionpolicy}%[CITE-CHECK],
and VLAs trained on limited demonstration data exhibit similar failure modes that produce near-zero actions. Action collapse itself is well recognized. Its interaction with displacement-based safety metrics is not: a collapsed model registers as maximally safe because it generates no motion that could cause collisions. CAR cannot distinguish a model that plans a collision-free trajectory from a model that does nothing.

All collision avoidance methods reviewed in Section~\ref{sec:rw_collision} adopt CAR without examining its construct validity. Our displacement-filtered variant, CAR$_\text{f}$ (Section~\ref{sec:metrics}), conditions safety measurement on sufficient motor activity and converts CAR from a contaminated aggregate into a metric that isolates genuine avoidance from inaction.

2	
3	At first glance, the collision avoidance results for SDF-augmented VLA models appear compelling. Our A1-LoRA model (Pi0 fine-tuned with an SDF auxiliary loss) achieves a Collision Avoidance Rate (CAR) of 91.5\% across 800 evaluation episodes on the SafeLIBERO benchmark~\cite{hu2025vlsa}, a figure that would suggest reliable obstacle avoidance. When we examine the end-effector displacement of the 732 episodes classified as ``safe,'' the picture changes entirely: 541 episodes (73.9\%) exhibit a maximum displacement below 1\,$\mu$m, and another 188 episodes (25.7\%) remain below 0.1\,mm. 19	# 论文写作风格规范
20	
21	> 核心哲学：**论文是一个有说服力的故事，不是实验报告。** 审稿人在几十秒内判断论文价值——如果 Abstract 和 Introduction 读起来像实验日志，论文就已经失败了。
22	
23	---
24	
25	## 一、总体写作哲学
26	
27	### 1.1 故事驱动，不是数据堆砌
28	
29	- 论文必须以"故事线"为核心展开：问题 → 洞察 → 方法 → 验证
30	- 禁止大量实验数据堆砌——每个数字出现必须服务于叙事推进
31	- 附录内容必须在正文中有明确引用且融入叙事，禁止简单堆砌
32	- 如果附录数据对核心叙事有重大影响，根据附录数据调整论文 framing
33	
34	### 1.2 主线统一性
35	
36	- 当 idea 在研究过程中发生变化后，**必须重审全文逻辑**
37	- 常见问题：Introduction 讲的故事 A，Method 做的是故事 B，Results 又在讲故事 C
38	- 修复方式：从最终实验结论反推，重写 Introduction 的问题定义和动机
39	- 每次 idea 调整后检查：Abstract → Introduction → Method → Results → Discussion → Conclusion 是否形成一条连贯主线
40	
41	### 1.3 专有名词必须有定义
42	
43	- 首次出现的专有名词/缩写必须给出完整定义和解释
44	- Abstract 中使用的缩写也必须在 Abstract 内定义（如 LLM = Large Language Model）
45	- 不能假设读者知道你自己定义的术语——论文从来没解释过的概念不能直接使用
46	- 通用规则：如果一个非标准术语第一次出现时没有括号定义，就是写作 bug
47	
48	### 1.4 写作前必读同类优秀论文
49	
50	- 每个章节动笔前，找 **2-3 篇目标会议近 1-2 年的高分论文**作为风格参考——同类问题或同类方法皆可
51	- 重点学：
52	  - Abstract 怎么用最少篇幅讲完故事
53	  - Introduction 怎么从大问题切入到具体贡献
54	  - Related Work 怎么 positioning 自己（不是 survey）
55	  - Table/Figure 怎么压缩信息密度
56	- **不是抄袭**，是学习同行的故事节奏和审美——不同子领域叙事节奏差异很大
57	- 实操：Paper Agent 可以从 `literature_map.yaml` 中挑 `role=foundation` 或 `role=direct-competitor` 的论文，把 `{title, venue, year, abstract}` 附在 Worker 的 task_prompt 中作为概念参考；如需学习写作风格本身，让 Worker 通过 WebSearch 取得论文链接并 fetch 全文
